opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, it comes down to the kind of problems I enjoy and where I think I can have the most leverage.

When I started out, I was drawn to a lot of different parts of AI, including modeling, algorithms, and evaluation. But I kept noticing that the bottleneck often wasn't a lack of ideas. It was whether those ideas could run efficiently, reliably, and at scale. A brilliant model that's too slow or too expensive to serve doesn't really reach people. Infrastructure is the layer that turns research into something usable.

I also like that infrastructure problems are very concrete. You can measure them. Latency goes down, throughput goes up, memory usage drops, and you know whether you've made progress. That feedback loop really suits how I think. I enjoy digging into the details of scheduling, caching, and how computation actually maps onto hardware. There's a craftsmanship to it that I find satisfying.

The other part is leverage. If you build a good serving system or runtime, every model and every application on top of it benefits. One improvement in the system can help thousands of developers at once, and it often unlocks things that weren't practical before, like longer contexts, more complex agent workflows, or running large models on cheaper hardware. That multiplier effect is very motivating.

Finally, I think infrastructure sits at a nice intersection. You need to understand the models well enough to know what matters, and you need to understand systems and hardware well enough to make it fast. I like working at that boundary, talking to model researchers on one side and systems people on the other, and figuring out how to make the whole stack work together. That's where I feel I fit best.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to what I actually enjoy on a day-to-day basis, and also where I think I can make a difference. With model research, a lot of the work is about chasing a frontier that moves very fast, and honestly the outcome depends a lot on compute and timing and a bit of luck. You can run a huge number of experiments and end up with results that are hard to attribute to anything you specifically did. Infrastructure is different. When I make a serving system faster, or get memory usage down, or make scheduling smarter, I can measure it. The improvement is real and it stays real.

The other thing is that I like problems that are concrete. Systems work has a very clear feedback loop: you profile, you find the bottleneck, you fix it, you see the number go up. That kind of engineering satisfaction is something I've always been drawn to, even back in school. Model research is often more about intuition and taste, and I respect people who are great at it, but it's not where I'm strongest.

And then there's the leverage argument. Every model, no matter who trains it, has to be served. If you make inference twice as cheap, that benefit flows to everyone building on top of it, whether they're a big lab or a small startup or a student running something on a single GPU. That open, shared nature of infrastructure is something I care about a lot, which is part of why I've been drawn to open-source projects like SGLang. You're not competing on one model that might be obsolete in six months. You're building the layer that everything else stands on.

I'd also say the field was actually under-invested for a while. Everyone wanted to do model work, and the systems side, especially inference, had a lot of low-hanging fruit. So it felt like a place where a relatively small team with the right ideas could have an outsized impact. That's still true today, maybe even more so as models get bigger and the economics of serving them become the real constraint.

For me, infrastructure is a good fit because I enjoy thinking about systems—how the pieces fit together, where the bottlenecks are, and how to make the whole thing work more efficiently. In AI, a model’s capabilities are only part of the picture. You also have to make it reliable, affordable, and easy for people to use.

I like that infrastructure gives you concrete problems to work on, but solving them can have a broad impact. If you improve the underlying system, you can help many different applications. That combination of technical depth and practical impact is what draws me to it.
